subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: In this unit you will go further with time. You will name the seven days of the week and the twelve months of the year in the correct order, use yesterday, today and tomorrow correctly, and read both o'clock and half past times on a clock face.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 1 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Name the seven days of the week in the correct order.
Name the twelve months of the year in the correct order.
Use the words yesterday, today and tomorrow correctly.
Say what day comes before or after a given day.
Say what month comes before or after a given month.
Read o'clock times on a clock face (minute hand on 12).
Read half past times on a clock face (minute hand on 6).
Tell the difference between the hour hand (short) and the minute hand (long).
Put simple daily events in order using time words.

concepts.title: The Days of the Week
concepts.explanation: There are seven days, and they always come in the same order, like a wheel that turns round and round. After Sunday comes Monday again — the week never stops turning. Most of the day names even end in the same sound, ‘day’, which children love to notice.
concepts.example: Play ‘what comes next?’ and ‘what came before?’ often. Say a day and ask yourself for the one after it, then the one before it. When they are confident going forwards, challenge them to say the days backwards — this really shows they know the order and are not just reciting a memorised song. Keep it playful: pause before the last day and shout it out.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Sing the days as a chant to a tune you know, clapping once for each day: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Lay out seven stones in a line, one for each day, and touch each stone as you say its name. Tie the days to real events you recognise: ‘Friday is Jummah,’ ‘Saturday and Sunday we are at home,’ ‘Monday we go back to school.’ Point to today on a calendar every single day, then to yesterday just behind it and tomorrow just ahead. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Let us sing the days. Clap with me! Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.” You: “Today is Saturday. What day was yesterday?” Child: “Friday!” You: “Yes — Jummah. And what day will it be tomorrow?” Child: “Sunday!”

concepts.title: Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow
concepts.explanation:
These three words are how you talk about time moving from one day to the next.

Today is the day you are in right now. Yesterday is the day that has already gone — it finished when you went to sleep. Tomorrow is the day still to come, the one that begins when you wake up again.

These words are easy to muddle at first, so the best way to learn them is to use them out loud, many times a day, about real things that happen to you. Say what you did yesterday, what you are doing today, and what you will do tomorrow.

Notice that the words move along with you. The day you called tomorrow becomes today when you wake up, and then becomes yesterday the day after that.
concepts.example: Say this out loud, filling in your own days: 'Today is Tuesday. Yesterday was Monday. Tomorrow will be Wednesday.' Then say one thing you did yesterday and one thing you will do tomorrow.

concepts.title: The Months of the Year
concepts.explanation: There are twelve months in a year, and they always come in the same order: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December. After December the year starts again at January. Saying them in order — clapping the beat as you go — helps you remember them, and laying twelve stones out in a circle shows you how the year comes back round to where it started.
concepts.example: Notice patterns together, because patterns make memory easy. Two days of the week begin with S (Saturday and Sunday). Two months begin with the letter A (April and August). Spotting these little rhymes and matches turns a long list into something you can play with rather than simply memorise.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Chant the months in order, clapping the beat: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December. Use a months wheel or lay out twelve stones in a circle so you see that after December we come back round to January. Ask gentle ‘what comes next?’ questions: ‘It is April now — which month comes next?’ Do not expect a young child to know all twelve quickly; going forwards from a given month is a fine first step. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Let us say the months and clap. January, February, March, April…” You: “It is February now. Which month comes next?” Child: “March!” You: “Well done. And which special month do we fast in?” Child: “Ramadan!”

concepts.title: Reading O'Clock Times
concepts.explanation: A clock face has two hands. The short hand is the hour hand and the long hand is the minute hand. When we say a time is ‘o'clock’, it is exactly on the hour: the long hand points straight up to the 12, and the short hand points right at a number. Whatever number the short hand points to is the hour we say.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Make the paper-plate clock together. Set the long hand on the 12 and move the short hand to the 3: ‘The long hand is on 12, the short hand is on 3, so it is 3 o'clock.’ move the hands and say the time. Always begin with o'clock times before half past — get this rock solid first. The very first job is telling the two hands apart, so keep repeating ‘short hand for the hour, long hand for the minutes’. Tie each time to something you do. ‘We wake for Fajr. School starts at 8 o'clock. We eat lunch at 12 o'clock. Bedtime is at 8 o'clock at night.’ When a time on the clock means something real, you care about reading it. Point at the real clock in the home whenever a familiar moment arrives and ask, ‘What does the clock say now?’

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Look at our clock. The long hand is pointing to the 12. That means it is o'clock.” You: “Now, where is the short hand pointing?” Child: “The 8!” You: “So the time is 8 o'clock — time for school. You read the clock!”

concepts.title: Reading Half Past Times
concepts.explanation: Half past means halfway through the hour — thirty minutes after it. On the clock, the long minute hand points straight down to the 6 (the bottom of the clock), and the short hour hand sits halfway between two numbers. We say ‘half past’ and then the number the hour hand has just gone past.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: On the paper-plate clock, move the long hand from the 12 all the way down to the 6 and watch how the short hand slides to sit between two numbers. Set half past 2: long hand on 6, short hand between the 2 and the 3, so it is ‘half past 2’. The tricky part for children is that the hour hand is no longer pointing straight at a number — remind them we say the number it has just passed, not the one ahead. Showing ‘half of the circle’ by tracing your finger from 12 down to 6 helps the idea of ‘halfway’ feel real. Connect half past to real moments too: ‘We leave for school at half past 7,’ ‘snack is at half past 3,’ ‘we get ready for bed at half past 8.’ Practise switching between o'clock and half past on the same clock so you watch the long hand jump between the 12 and the 6.

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “The long hand is pointing down to the 6. That means half past.” You: “The short hand is between the 3 and the 4. Which number did it just pass?” Child: “The 3!” You: “So it is half past 3 — time for our snack. Wonderful reading!”

concepts.title: Putting Events in Order
concepts.explanation: Time is also about sequence — what comes first, next and last. Someone who can order the events of their day is building the same ‘what comes next?’ thinking they use for days, months and clock times. Talk through the day in order: ‘First we pray Fajr, then we eat breakfast, then we go to school, then we come home, then we sleep.’
concepts.example: Thinking the days or months can start anywhere. Remember the order never changes; after Sunday always comes Monday, after December always comes January.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: say your day in order, using words like first, next, then and last. Mix it up by naming two events and asking which happens first — ‘Which comes first, breakfast or bedtime?’ Link it to the clock: ‘Breakfast is at 8 o'clock, and dinner is at 7 o'clock in the evening — which one is earlier in the day?’ Confusing the two hands. You read the minute hand as the hour. Keep repeating ‘short hand = hour, long hand = minutes’ and use hands of different lengths or colours. Saying the wrong hour for half past. At half past 3 the hour hand sits between 3 and 4, and some children say ‘half past 4’. Remind them we name the number the hour hand has just passed. Muddling yesterday and tomorrow. These take time. Use them in real sentences every day, always pointing to a calendar. Losing the order of days or months. This is normal — the cure is cheerful repetition through songs, chants and wheels, not testing under pressure.

explorations.title: The Days of the Week
explorations.context: There are seven days, and they always come in the same order, like a wheel that turns round and round. After Sunday comes Monday again — the week never stops turning. Most of the day names even end in the same sound, ‘day’, which children love to notice.
explorations.prompt: What day comes right after Sunday?
explorations.hint: Remember, the week is like a wheel — after Sunday it turns back to the start.
explorations.explanation: The seven days always come in the same order and loop back to Monday after Sunday, like a wheel that keeps turning rather than a line that stops. Chanting them with a clap for each day, and touching a stone or card as each name is said, helps the order stick before you are asked to recall it alone.

explorations.title: Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow
explorations.context: These three words are how a small child first feels time moving. Today is now, yesterday is the day that has gone, and tomorrow is the day still to come. Children often muddle them, so use them out loud many times a day in real situations.
explorations.prompt: If today is Wednesday, what day was yesterday?
explorations.hint: Yesterday is the day that came just before today.
explorations.explanation: These three words anchor your sense of time passing: today is happening now, yesterday has already gone, and tomorrow is still ahead. Because they are easy to muddle, use them in real sentences about real events — meals, prayers, outings — many times a day, not only during the lesson.

explorations.title: The Months of the Year
explorations.context: A year has twelve months, always in the same order: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December. After December comes January again.
explorations.prompt: It is April now. Which month comes next?
explorations.hint: Say the months in order and listen for the one right after April.
explorations.explanation: The twelve months follow the same idea as the days of the week — a fixed order that loops back to January after December — so the same chanting and circling technique applies, just with a longer list.
explorations.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Chant the months in order, clapping the beat: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December.

Start by asking only 'what comes next?' from a month the child already knows well, such as the current one, rather than expecting the full list right away.

explorations.title: Reading O'Clock Times
explorations.context: A clock face has two hands. The short hand is the hour hand and the long hand is the minute hand. When we say a time is ‘o'clock’, it is exactly on the hour: the long hand points straight up to the 12, and the short hand points right at a number.
explorations.prompt: The long hand points to the 12 and the short hand points to the 3. What time is it?
explorations.hint: When the long hand is on 12, read the number the short hand points to.
explorations.explanation: An o'clock time is easy to spot because the long minute hand always points straight up at the 12; whatever number the short hour hand rests on is the hour we say. Tying each o'clock time to something real in your day — school starting at 8, lunch at 12 — gives the number on the clock a meaning worth remembering.

explorations.title: Reading Half Past Times
explorations.context: Half past means halfway through the hour — thirty minutes after it. On the clock, the long minute hand points straight down to the 6 (the bottom of the clock), and the short hour hand sits halfway between two numbers.
explorations.prompt: The long hand points to the 6 and the short hand sits between the 2 and the 3. What time is it?
explorations.hint: Long hand on 6 means half past — say the number the short hand has just passed.
explorations.explanation: Half past means the long minute hand has swept all the way down to point at the 6, while the short hour hand has moved on from the last hour but not yet reached the next one. We name the hour the short hand has just passed, not the one it is heading toward — practising o'clock and half past on the same clock face makes that difference easy to see.

explorations.title: Putting Events in Order
explorations.context: Time is also about sequence — what comes first, next and last. Someone who can order the events of their day is building the same ‘what comes next?’ thinking they use for days, months and clock times.
explorations.prompt: First we pray Fajr, then we eat breakfast, then we go to school. What do we do first?
explorations.hint: Look for the word 'first' in the story.
explorations.explanation: Ordering a day's events uses the exact same thinking as ordering days or months: working out what comes first, next and last. Asking you to retell your own day, then naming two events out of order and asking which happens first, checks whether they have really understood the sequence rather than just memorised it.

methods.title: Chant and Touch the Days of the Week
methods.example: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday — then the week starts again at Monday.
steps: Chant the seven days in order together, clapping once for each day: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.
Lay out seven stones or cards in a line and touch one for each day as you say its name, so you see there are always seven.
Say the days alone starting from Monday, then check together that none was skipped or repeated.

methods.title: Talk Through Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow
methods.example: If today is Wednesday, yesterday was Tuesday and tomorrow will be Thursday.
steps: Say the day's name out loud each morning: 'Today is ___.'
Ask yourself what day came before (yesterday) and what day comes next (tomorrow), using a real event to anchor each answer.
Repeat the three words in a real sentence at different times of day, such as at breakfast and bedtime, until you use them without help.

methods.title: Chant the Months and Circle Back to January
methods.example: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December — then the year begins again.
steps: Chant the twelve months in order, clapping the beat, using a months wheel or twelve stones set out in a circle.
Point to each stone as you say its month, then show that after December the circle returns to January.
Ask yourself 'what comes next?' starting from a month you already know, such as this one.

methods.title: Build and Read a Paper-Plate Clock for O'Clock Times
methods.example: Long hand on the 12, short hand on the 3: it is 3 o'clock.
steps: Make a paper-plate clock with a short hour hand and a long minute hand.
Set the long hand straight up on the 12, then move the short hand to point at a number, and say the time together: 'long hand on 12, short hand on 3, so it is 3 o'clock.'
Move the short hand to a new number and say the new o'clock time themselves.

methods.title: Move the Long Hand to the 6 for Half Past
methods.example: Long hand on the 6, short hand resting between the 2 and the 3: it is half past 2.
steps: On the paper-plate clock, move the long hand from the 12 down to the 6 and watch the short hand slide to sit between two numbers.
Say the rule together: 'half past' and then the number the short hand has just passed.
Practise switching between o'clock and half past on the same clock so you compare the two hand positions.

methods.title: Retell the Day in Order
methods.example: First we pray Fajr, then we eat breakfast, then we go to school, then we come home, then we sleep.
steps: Say your day in order, using the words first, next, then and last.
Name two events from the day and ask yourself which one happens first.
Check the order together and fix any event that was placed in the wrong spot.

workedExamples.title: Saying the days of the week in order
workedExamples.prompt: Say the Days of the Week in Order
workedExamples.solution: Say the seven days from the start: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Clap once for each day as you say it, then check that all seven were said and none was repeated.

workedExamples.title: Yesterday and tomorrow from Wednesday
workedExamples.solution: Today is Wednesday. The day before today is Tuesday, so yesterday was Tuesday. The day after today is Thursday, so tomorrow will be Thursday.

workedExamples.title: Saying the months of the year in order
workedExamples.prompt: Say the Months of the Year in Order
workedExamples.solution: Say the twelve months from the start: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December. After December, the year begins again at January.

workedExamples.title: Reading an o'clock time
workedExamples.solution: The long hand points straight up to the 12 and the short hand points at the 7. The long hand on 12 tells us it is exactly on the hour, and the short hand tells us which hour — so the time is 7 o'clock.

workedExamples.title: Reading a half past time
workedExamples.solution: The long hand points straight down to the 6, which tells us it is half past the hour. The short hand sits between the 4 and the 5, so it has just passed the 4 — the time is half past 4.

workedExamples.title: Putting a morning in order
workedExamples.solution: Look at the four events: waking up, eating breakfast, walking to school, and sitting in class. First we wake up, next we eat breakfast, then we walk to school, and last we sit in class.

workedExamples.title: Counting one day back and one forward
workedExamples.prompt: The Day Before and After Thursday
workedExamples.solution: Thursday is the day. Counting back one day from Thursday gives Wednesday, so the day before Thursday is Wednesday. Counting forward one day from Thursday gives Friday, so the day after Thursday is Friday.

workedExamples.title: Counting one month back and one forward
workedExamples.prompt: The Month Before and After June
workedExamples.solution: June is the month. Counting back one month from June gives May, so the month before June is May. Counting forward one month from June gives July, so the month after June is July.

workedExamples.title: Naming tomorrow from today
workedExamples.solution: Today is Tuesday. The day after Tuesday, going in order Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, is Wednesday, so tomorrow is Wednesday.

workedExamples.title: Naming yesterday from today
workedExamples.solution: Today is Sunday. The day before Sunday, going back through the week Saturday, Sunday, is Saturday, so yesterday was Saturday.

workedExamples.title: Finding the missing month
workedExamples.prompt: ★ The Missing Month: April, May, ____, July
workedExamples.solution: The months go in order April, May, June, July. The missing month between May and July is June.

workedExamples.title: Reading the time from the clock hands
workedExamples.prompt: ★ Read the Time: Long Hand on 12, Short Hand on 9
workedExamples.solution: The long hand is on the 12, so the time is exactly on the hour. The short hand points at the 9, so the time is 9 o'clock.

practice.prompt: Say the days of the week in order, starting from Monday.
practice.answer: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.
practice.hint: Start at Monday and count the days on your fingers, one finger for each day.

practice.prompt: If today is Friday, what day is tomorrow?
practice.hint: Tomorrow is the day that comes straight after today.

practice.prompt: Say the months of the year in order, starting from January.
practice.answer: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December.
practice.hint: Chant the months the way you practised with your teacher, one clap per month.

practice.prompt: The long hand points to the 12 and the short hand points to the 5. What time is it?
practice.hint: When the long hand is on the 12, the time is exactly on the hour — read the number the short hand points to.

practice.prompt: Fill in the missing day: Monday, Tuesday, ____, Thursday, Friday.
practice.hint: Say the days in order out loud and listen for the one that is missing.
Say the days in order out loud: the first blank comes between Monday and Wednesday, and the second blank comes right after Thursday.

practice.prompt: What day comes right after Friday?
practice.hint: Say the days in order starting from Friday and listen for the very next one.

practice.prompt: Today is Thursday. What day was yesterday, and what day is tomorrow?
practice.answer: Yesterday was Wednesday and tomorrow is Friday.
practice.hint: Yesterday comes just before today, and tomorrow comes just after today.
Find Tuesday in the week and say the day that comes straight after it.
Find Sunday in the week and say the day that comes straight before it.

practice.prompt: Fill in the missing month: April, May, ____, July.
practice.hint: Say the months in order out loud and listen for the one that is missing.

practice.prompt: What month comes right after August?
practice.hint: Say the months in order starting from August and listen for the very next one.

activities.title: Practise together
activities.materials: Paper, pencil and familiar household objects
steps: Choose one idea from this unit.
Build or draw a model of it.
Explain your model to a family member.
Write one question of your own and solve it.

rules.title: The Days of the Week
rules.text: There are seven days, and they always come in the same order, like a wheel that turns round and round.

rules.title: Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow
rules.text: These three words are how a small child first feels time moving.

rules.title: The Months of the Year
rules.text: The twelve months always come in the same order: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December. Chanting them in order, clapping the beat, is the quickest way to learn them.
rules.grownUpGuide:
The Months of the Year

How to teach it: Chant the months in order, clapping the beat: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December.

rules.title: Reading O'Clock Times
rules.text: A clock face has two hands.

rules.title: Reading Half Past Times
rules.text: Half past means halfway through the hour — thirty minutes after it.

rules.title: Putting Events in Order
rules.text: Time is also about sequence — what comes first, next and last.

terms: The day it is right now
One of the twelve parts of a year
A time exactly on the hour
The short hand — points to the hour
The long hand — points to the minutes
commonMistakes: A common mistake is answering with a different day, such as Sunday, because it feels like a special day
Re-read the sentence: it names Friday.
A common mistake is saying the market trip happens after today
Yesterday always means a day that has already gone, so it happened before today.
A common mistake is answering 'March' by naming the month before April instead of after
The month right after April is May.
A common mistake is counting today as one of the days to wait
Since today is Thursday, Jummah (Friday) is the very next day, so it is 1 day away, not 2.
A common mistake is saying the test is today
Today is Tuesday, and the test day (Wednesday) is the day after today, so it is tomorrow.

fluency.hint: Say the days in order starting from Monday.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is answering 'Wednesday' by skipping a day — go one day at a time: Monday, then Tuesday.

fluency.prompt: If today is Saturday, what day is tomorrow?
fluency.hint: Tomorrow is the very next day after today.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 'Friday' because it feels close to Saturday — tomorrow always comes after today, not before, so it is Sunday.

fluency.hint: Say the months in order starting from January.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is answering 'April', jumping ahead a month — go one month at a time: January, February, then March.

fluency.prompt: The long hand is on the 12 and the short hand is on the 2. What time is it?
fluency.hint: Long hand on 12 means it is exactly on the hour.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is reading the short hand as the minutes — the short hand tells the hour, so the time is 2 o'clock, not '12 o'clock'.

fluency.prompt: The long hand is on the 6 and the short hand is between the 7 and the 8. What time is it?
fluency.hint: Long hand on 6 means it is half past the hour.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 'half past 8' by reading the number the hand is closest to — the short hand has only just passed the 7, so it is half past 7.

fluency.prompt: We wake up, eat breakfast, then go to school. What happens first?
fluency.hint: The word first tells you the very first thing that happens.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is answering 'eating breakfast' — check the order again: waking up happens before breakfast, so it is first.

fluency.hint: Count back one day from Sunday.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 'Monday' because it comes after Sunday — the question asks for the day before, which is Saturday.

fluency.hint: Count back one month from December.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 'January' because it comes after December in the next year — the question asks for the month before, which is November.

fluency.prompt: Which clock hand is the hour hand — the short one or the long one?
fluency.hint: Remember: short hand for hours, long hand for minutes.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is thinking the long hand shows the hour because it looks more important — the short hand always shows the hour, the long hand shows the minutes.

fluency.prompt: Put these in order: eat lunch, wake up, go to school.
fluency.answer: Wake up, go to school, eat lunch.
fluency.hint: Think about which of these three things happens first in a normal day.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is listing them in the order they were said rather than the order they happen — check each event against a normal school day: waking up comes first, then school, then lunch.

fluency.hint: Say the days in order starting from Wednesday.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is answering 'Friday' by skipping a day — go one day at a time: Wednesday, then Thursday.

fluency.prompt: If today is Monday, what day was yesterday?
fluency.hint: Yesterday is the day that came just before today.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 'Tuesday' because it sounds like the next day — yesterday is always before today, so it is Sunday.

realProblems.prompt: At home, Amina helps her mother cook a special family meal every Friday. What day of the week is the special meal?
realProblems.hint: The day name is given in the story — find it and say it back.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is answering with a different day, such as Sunday, because it feels like a special day — re-read the sentence: it names Friday.

realProblems.prompt: Hodan's family went to the market yesterday, and today they are resting at home. Did the market trip happen before or after today?
realProblems.hint: The word yesterday always means the day before today.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying the market trip happens after today — yesterday always means a day that has already gone, so it happened before today.

realProblems.prompt: A family plans a trip to visit their grandparents. They leave in the month right after April. Which month do they travel?
realProblems.hint: Say the months in order and find the one straight after April.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is answering 'March' by naming the month before April instead of after — the month right after April is May.

realProblems.prompt: Yusuf goes to Friday prayers (Jummah) every week. If today is Thursday, how many days until Jummah?
realProblems.hint: Find today on the week and count forward to Friday.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is counting today as one of the days to wait — since today is Thursday, Jummah (Friday) is the very next day, so it is 1 day away, not 2.

realProblems.prompt: Ibrahim's class has a spelling test every Wednesday. Today is Tuesday. Is the spelling test today, or tomorrow?
realProblems.answer: Tomorrow — the test is on Wednesday.
realProblems.hint: Work out what day comes after Tuesday.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying the test is today — today is Tuesday, and the test day (Wednesday) is the day after today, so it is tomorrow.

realProblems.prompt: Fatima's family visits her grandmother on the first day of the week (Monday) and the last day of the week (Sunday). How many times a week does Fatima visit her grandmother?
realProblems.answer: Twice a week — once on Monday and once on Sunday.
realProblems.hint: Count how many separate days were named in the story.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is answering 'once' because it sounds like one visit — but two separate days were named, Monday and Sunday, so it is twice.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: If today is Saturday, what day is tomorrow? Explain using the words today and week in your answer.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Today is Saturday. A week always follows the same order, and after Saturday comes Sunday, so tomorrow is Sunday. Then the week starts again with Monday.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: If today is Wednesday, explain what yesterday was and what tomorrow will be.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Today is Wednesday. Yesterday is the day before today, so yesterday was Tuesday. Tomorrow is the day after today, so tomorrow will be Thursday.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Today is Tuesday. Explain how you worked out that tomorrow is Wednesday.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Today is Tuesday. To find tomorrow, I say the days in order and find the one that comes right after today: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. The day after Tuesday is Wednesday, so tomorrow is Wednesday.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Reading O'Clock Times.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A clock face has two hands. The short hand is the hour hand and the long hand is the minute hand. When we say a time is ‘o'clock’, it is exactly on the hour: the long hand points straight up to the 12, and the short hand points right at a number. Whatever number the short hand points to is the hour we say.
reasoningPrompts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Make the paper-plate clock together. Set the long hand on the 12 and move the short hand to the 3: ‘The long hand is on 12, the short hand is on 3, so it is 3 o'clock.’ move the hands and say the time. Always begin with o'clock times before half past — get this rock solid first. The very first job is telling the two hands apart, so keep repeating ‘short hand for the hour, long hand for the minutes’.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Reading Half Past Times.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Half past means halfway through the hour — thirty minutes after it. On the clock, the long minute hand points straight down to the 6 (the bottom of the clock), and the short hour hand sits halfway between two numbers. We say ‘half past’ and then the number the hour hand has just gone past.
reasoningPrompts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: On the paper-plate clock, move the long hand from the 12 all the way down to the 6 and watch how the short hand slides to sit between two numbers. Set half past 2: long hand on 6, short hand between the 2 and the 3, so it is ‘half past 2’. The tricky part for children is that the hour hand is no longer pointing straight at a number — remind them we say the number it has just passed, not the one ahead. Showing ‘half of the circle’ by tracing your finger from 12 down to 6 helps the idea of ‘halfway’ feel real.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Putting Events in Order.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Time is also about sequence — what comes first, next and last. Someone who can order the events of their day is building the same ‘what comes next?’ thinking they use for days, months and clock times. Talk through the day in order: ‘First we pray Fajr, then we eat breakfast, then we go to school, then we come home, then we sleep.’
reasoningPrompts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: say your day in order, using words like first, next, then and last. Mix it up by naming two events and asking which happens first — ‘Which comes first, breakfast or bedtime?’ Link it to the clock: ‘Breakfast is at 8 o'clock, and dinner is at 7 o'clock in the evening — which one is earlier in the day?’

questions.question: Which of these lists shows the days of the week in the correct order?
questions.hint: Say the days out loud in order and check which list matches.
questions.explanation: The days of the week always follow the same order: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.

questions.question: Today is Friday. What day is tomorrow?
questions.hint: Tomorrow is the day that comes right after today.
questions.explanation: Today is Friday, and the day right after Friday is Saturday, so tomorrow is Saturday.

questions.question: Which month comes right after March?
questions.hint: Say the months in order starting from January and find the one after March.
questions.explanation: The months go in order January, February, March, April — so April comes right after March.

questions.question: The long hand points to the 12 and the short hand points to the 6. What time is it?
questions.hint: When the long hand is on the 12, it is exactly on the hour.
questions.explanation: The long hand on the 12 means the time is exactly on the hour, and the short hand on the 6 tells us the hour, so it is 6 o'clock.

questions.question: The long hand points to the 6 and the short hand sits between the 3 and the 4. What time is it?
questions.hint: The long hand on the 6 means it is half past the hour that the short hand has just passed.
questions.explanation: The long hand on the 6 tells us it is half past the hour, and the short hand has just passed the 3, so the time is half past 3.

questions.question: Yusuf wakes up, then eats breakfast, then walks to school. What does he do last?
questions.hint: Look at the order the three events were told in the story.
questions.explanation: The events happen in this order: wake up, eat breakfast, walk to school — so walking to school is the last of the three.

questions.question: What day comes right before Saturday?
questions.hint: Say the days of the week in order and find the one just before Saturday.
questions.explanation: The days go in order Thursday, Friday, Saturday — so the day right before Saturday is Friday.

questions.question: What month comes right before September?
questions.hint: Say the months in order and find the one just before September.
questions.explanation: The months go in order July, August, September — so the month right before September is August.

questions.question: Today is Sunday. What day was yesterday?
questions.hint: Yesterday is the day that comes right before today.
questions.explanation: Today is Sunday, and the day right before Sunday is Saturday, so yesterday was Saturday.
